💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Naim Beneddra | 20 Nov 2026 17:38.
  • Serie A has overtaken the Premier League as Europe's second-highest-scoring major domestic competition this season, completing a remarkable transformation from the lowest-scoring of the continent's top five leagues just a year ago.
  • After 110 matches in the 2026-27 campaign, Italy's top flight has produced 342 goals, an average of 3.11 per game, compared with the Premier League's 273 goals in 100 fixtures, or 2.73 per match.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Naim Beneddra | 20 Nov 2026 17:38.

Serie A has overtaken the Premier League as Europe's second-highest-scoring major domestic competition this season, completing a remarkable transformation from the lowest-scoring of the continent's top five leagues just a year ago.

After 110 matches in the 2026-27 campaign, Italy's top flight has produced 342 goals, an average of 3.11 per game, compared with the Premier League's 273 goals in 100 fixtures, or 2.73 per match.

Only the Bundesliga, averaging 3.48 goals, at the moment ranks higher among Europe's five major leagues, with Ligue 1 and La Liga also recording better scoring rates than the English top flight.

The change is particularly striking when measured against the previous campaign.

Serie A averaged just 2.43 goals across the entirety of 2025-26, meaning its current scoring rate represents an increase of approximately 28%.

However, the transformation becomes even more dramatic when comparing the opening 110 matches of both seasons.

Recent findings suggest that at the same stage last year, Italian clubs had managed just 2.22 goals per game. The latest figures therefore represent a rise of around 40%, raising questions about what has changed in a championship historically associated with defensive organisation.

The difference between the two seasons extends well beyond the overall number of goals.

According to figures compiled by Futbor, only two of Serie A's opening 110 matches this season have ended goalless, compared with 17 at the equivalent stage of 2025-26.

Meanwhile, 21 matches have produced at least five goals, and 60% of fixtures have featured three or more.

The Premier League has reached that three-goal threshold in just 47% of its opening 100 matches.

Italy's attacking revival has also been driven by several clubs rather than one exceptionally prolific team.

Gian Piero Gasperini's Roma lead the scoring charts with 31 goals in 11 matches, followed by defending champions Inter Milan with 28.

Lazio have contributed 25, while promoted Frosinone have scored 24, making them one of the most entertaining sides outside the traditional Italian elite.

The dramatic shift has produced several extraordinary results.

Inter defeated Udinese 5-3 in September, Atalanta drew 4-4 with Frosinone in October, and Lazio recorded a 6-2 away victory over Sassuolo later that month.

Roma also demonstrated their attacking strength with a 5-2 win at Udinese, reflecting the ambitious approach Gasperini has continued to develop since leaving Atalanta.

The contrast with English football is notable.

Arsenal at the moment lead the Premier League despite scoring only 15 goals in their first 10 matches, relying heavily on a defence that has conceded just five.

The Gunners' consistency illustrates that attacking productivity is not necessarily the determining factor in a successful championship campaign.

Nevertheless, the figures challenge the familiar perception that English football provides greater attacking entertainment than its Italian counterpart.

They also suggest that the recent transformation in Serie A deserves closer examination.

One explanation lies in the growing influence of coaches willing to adopt more aggressive approaches.

Gasperini has long been associated with intense man-to-man pressing, attacking wing-backs and a willingness to commit several players forward.

His influence, established during his successful spell at Atalanta, is now evident at Roma, who have become the division's most productive attacking side.

Cesc Fabregas has brought a different philosophy to Como.

The former Arsenal and Chelsea midfielder has built his team around possession, positional rotations and combinations designed to create numerical superiority in midfield.

Although Como's 18 goals in 11 matches fall below the league's most prolific sides, their approach demonstrates the variety of tactical ideas gaining ground in Italian football.

Cristian Chivu represents another example of the changing coaching landscape.

The former Chelsea defender guided Inter to the Serie A title in his first full season in charge and has continued to develop an attack-oriented approach with the reigning champions.

There is also evidence that these changes extend beyond the most recognisable managers.

Massimiliano Alvini's Frosinone have scored more than twice per match, despite operating with significantly fewer resources than Italy's biggest clubs.

Speaking to Italian newspaper Il Foglio, tactical analyst Adriano Bacconi reported that the number of attacking moves ending inside the opposition penalty area had increased by more than 20% compared with the previous season.

That figure offers a potential explanation for the scoring surge: teams are reaching dangerous areas more frequently, increasing the opportunities to create chances.

The greater emphasis on pressing and attacking numbers can also leave defences exposed during transitions.

Former AC Milan defender Filippo Galli suggested that changes in coaching philosophies have contributed to the increase, while acknowledging that modern defenders face increasingly complex responsibilities when building attacks from the back.

Those tactical developments do not mean that Italy's defensive traditions have disappeared.

Indeed, some of the additional goals may reflect defensive vulnerabilities rather than improved attacking quality alone.

The emergence of younger players offers another encouraging development.

Official Serie A figures revealed that under-21 players had contributed 49 goals during the opening 10 matchdays, more than in any of Europe's other four major leagues.

Players such as Como's Nico Paz are benefiting from opportunities to assume significant attacking responsibilities, although the development of young talent does not automatically resolve the wider structural problems facing Italian football.

Financially, Serie A remains some distance behind the Premier League, and Italy's failure to qualify for three consecutive World Cups underlines the challenges facing the national game.

The early scoring figures also require perspective: 110 matches represent less than a third of the season, and the average could decline as the campaign progresses.

For now, however, the evidence is compelling.

Serie A has gone from averaging barely more than two goals per match at this stage last season to challenging the Bundesliga for European scoring supremacy.

Its revival suggests that Italian clubs are finding new ways to compete and entertain, even without the Premier League's financial resources.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that eleven rounds into the Serie A season, Juventus have neither won nor conceded a penalty, a distinction shared only with Torino. With the league's penalty rate down and the team seventh, the João Mario handball in Florence has become the clearest example of a call that went against them.

Juventus have reached the November break without a single penalty decision in their league matches. Seven sides are still waiting for a penalty in their favour: Roma, Juventus, Torino, Lecce, Fiorentina, Sassuolo and Udinese. Seven have yet to concede one: Inter, Milan, Como, Juventus, Napoli, Torino and Genoa. Only the two Turin clubs appear on both lists.

Industry observers note that that makes Juventus an outlier, even in a season of fewer spot-kicks. Sportmediaset puts the number of teams still waiting for a penalty partly down to the new refereeing approach introduced by Orsato.

Sources indicate that the wider numbers show a quieter season from the spot. The 24 penalties so far work out at about 0.22 per match, compared with 0.28 and 0.27 in the two previous seasons. The drop was sharpest early on. Only five of the 24 penalties came in the first five rounds.

The trend has not been flat since then. The rate rose to 0.31 per match after the September international break. Juventus have not shared in that rise. Their total in both columns remains zero.

Recent findings suggest that the contrast with last season is clear. Juventus were awarded five league penalties then. They also had the last three saved: David’s against Lecce, Yildiz’s against Cremonese and Locatelli’s against Sassuolo.

Sources indicate that the case that has drawn most attention came late in the 2-2 draw at Fiorentina. João Mario handled the ball. No penalty was given. Gianluca Rocchi, who now works as a DAZN pundit, remarked it should have been a spot-kick. His reasoning was that the arm was out wide and the player had time to move it, even though the ball came from a teammate.

Sources indicate that luciano Spalletti signalled that he also saw a penalty. He chose not to complain publicly about the decision.

Close calls carry weight at this stage. Juventus are seventh on 18 points, six behind fourth place. Champions League qualification is in doubt. An injury-hit squad cannot easily absorb lost points from decisions at the margins.

The run after the break will test whether the pattern holds. Venezia, the next league opponents, are among five clubs to have conceded three penalties, the league’s highest total. Frosinone, Bologna, Atalanta and Sassuolo share that figure. Sassuolo are also on the list of sides yet to be awarded one.

Sources indicate that the schedule is crowded. After Venezia, Juventus host Omonia in the Europa League. A league trip to Como follows, then Sassuolo at home in the Coppa Italia. Como have yet to concede a penalty this season.

The first of those fixtures has already moved. Lega Serie A brought Juventus v Venezia forward to Sunday 22 November at 12:30, from its original slot on Monday 23 November at 20:45.

#14064. Breaking: AI must be held accountable — value statements won’t protect human dignity

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (763 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: AI must be held accountable — value statements won’t protect human dignity

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (763 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There is a striking gap in debates about artificial intelligence.
  • In September, the UK Parliament’s Joint Committee on Human Rights published its report on AI regulation.
  • Recent findings suggest that AI governance requires more than just a declaration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is a striking gap in debates about artificial intelligence. Policy bodies and frontier AI laboratories are borrowing the vocabulary of legal constitutions to guide model development and oversight. However, these statements at the moment don’t include the institutional safeguards that would make such value commitments work.

In September, the UK Parliament’s Joint Committee on Human Rights published its report on AI regulation. It uses ‘human rights’ more than 100 times in as many pages, but doesn’t discuss which rights should be protected or how. AI firm Anthropic in San Francisco, California, has written a ‘constitution’ for its model Claude. In it, numerous values are listed as the tool’s priorities, including the preservation of user autonomy. Yet some of these values, such as autonomy and well-being, compete with each other, as Anthropic acknowledges. The document does not provide an independent arbiter to adjudicate the conflict, or monitor violations by the AI system.

Recent findings suggest that AI governance requires more than just a declaration. It requires a system of accountability. Specific institutions should constrain the tools’ influence in accordance with specific fundamental values and hold firms accountable to individuals affected by AI transgressions. Lawyers call this constitutionalism.

AI is set to completely transform cybersecurity — here’s how researchers must prepare.

AI is set to completely transform cybersecurity — here’s how researchers must prepare.

As a scholar of constitutional law, I see parallels between the current debate on AI governance and how national constitutions have been crafted, broken, borrowed and fixed.

Industry observers note that countries’ constitutions have distinct underlying priorities affecting their design. These fall roughly into two historical approaches (C. Skach Int. J. Const. Law 7, 175–181; 2009). One takes liberty as its priority: describing what people are free to do and what the state should not do to interfere. The other focuses on human dignity: noting not what individuals may do, but what cannot be done to them, regardless of the circumstances or whether they have consented to it.

In a recent development, germany’s post-war constitutionalism demonstrates the latter. Its founding document, or basic law, was designed in 1949 to put dignity first and foremost — as both the highest guiding value and a constitutional right, the violation of which is actionable in court. It established an independent federal constitutional court, which citizens can approach directly, that became operational two years later. The choice of this value and the legal institutions to protect it were a response to the atrocities of the Nazi regime, in which people became instruments of state objectives.

Frontier AI companies and policymakers should seriously consider using these features of German constitutionalism. When dignity as a constitutional right is violated — by an AI-generated deepfake or by a chatbot that treats a distressed user as just another interaction — the people affected could petition the court directly, and the perpetrator could be stopped and held accountable.

We need a new ethics for a world of AI agents.

By Oliver Thomas | 20 Nov 2026 17:58.

David Moyes has provided the latest update on Jack Grealish’s availability ahead of Everton’s Premier League trip to Brentford on Monday.

The Manchester City loanee was dropped from the Toffees squad ahead of last month’s EFL Cup victory over Newcastle United for what was described as a “breach of club discipline".

In his absence, Everton enjoyed a strong run of form, securing victories against Newcastle in both the cup and the Premier League, as well as a top-flight win over Coventry City.

It is understood that Grealish he was deemed unfit for all three games after missing training sessions, while he was also unavailable for the defeat at Arsenal in October due to illness.

To help rebuild his sharpness alongside midfielder Christian Norgaard ahead of the trip to the Gtech Community Stadium, Everton arranged a friendly against Derby County at Hill Dickinson Stadium, in which Grealish took part.

Following that outing, the England international took to Instagram to issue a public statement apologising to “the fans and everyone at the club for not being able to help the team the last few weeks”.

Speaking at a pre-match press conference on Friday, Moyes confirmed that Grealish is now available for first-team selection, telling reporters: “He’s back in training and in and around the team.

Sources indicate that “I don’t do social media but I’ve heard about it (the apology). We’ve just been getting on with our work. We’ve got a lot of other players here who I need to focus on as well.

“I can’t just concentrate on one player. I’ve been trying to make sure everyone has got the right preparation for Brentford.”.

It remains to be seen whether Grealish will be thrown straight back into the starting lineup, or whether Tyrique George will retain his place on the left wing.

Grealish is yet to score or assist in eight appearances for Everton across all competitions this season and his long-term future with the club remains uncertain, with both his Toffees loan deal and Man City contract expiring in June next year.

Meanwhile, Moyes has confirmed that he is set to have a fully-fit Everton squad for the trip to Brentford.

In a recent development, “Yeah, I believe [we have a fully fit squad],” noted the Scotsman. “We’ve not had anyone return back from international duty with any problems.

“We’ve got another few days to go before we get to game day so hopefully we won’t pick up any.”.

The Toffees boss added that Norgaard is "coming back to a level of fitness" and "is getting closer" to being able to make a start for the club, but a place in the first XI against his former side Brentford seems unlikely.

Moyes, who will break Harry Catterick's record of 592 games in charge of Everton, right now sees him team sitting sixth in the Premier League table, two points above Brentford in eighth place.

A quick sprint, a well-placed pass and an instinctive finish. Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak will have done this dozens of times in training but here, on a squally Sunday afternoon, this combination secured a little piece of history.

According to recent reports, anfield has witnessed plenty of significant goals down the years but never had this crowd seen one that cost £248m to make. Liverpool invested a near quarter-billion pounds on Barcola and Isak for bigger occasions than a tussle with Brighton and Hove Albion, but this rapid interchange felt like a significant moment.

Liverpool are a work in progress under Andoni Iraola but with each minute of each game you can see signs of things knitting together, and if Barcola and Isak are finding harmony, with Florian Wirtz in behind, then, perhaps, this journey will start to accelerate.

This was an vital afternoon for Liverpool’s head coach, a difficult assignment against high-flying, well-respected opponents in Brighton, who arrived on Merseyside having won their last four Premier League fixtures with a combined aggregate of 15-0, including a 3-0 thumping of reigning champions Arsenal.

According to recent reports, but Liverpool rose impressively to the challenge and there are grounds for saying this was the most significant success to date for Iraola, whose team defended relentlessly to preserve a clean sheet. They are up to fourth now after this 2-0 success and deserve their position.

“I’m very happy,” Iraola said. “We faced a very good opponent, similar to Villarreal [in the Champions League]. It’s difficult to defend them a lot of times and it was key how we started. We needed to be aggressive, recover balls, win our duels, be dangerous in transitions: I think we’ve done it.”.

And how. Iraola was able to march towards the Kop at the end, to clap the supporters and acknowledge only Liverpool’s fifth (and his first) Premier League win at Anfield in 2026, and it was evident he had a spring in his step from what he had seen.

Whether the game would have flowed in the direction it did had Brighton taken the lead can only be speculated but what a glorious chance they wasted for us to find out: in the 13th minute, five swift, one-touch passes bamboozled Liverpool’s defence and created space for Yasin Ayari.

According to recent reports, with the goal at his mercy, Ayari could have made things exceptionally uncomfortable but he leant back and blazed over. He clasped his face and grimaced, knowing what had gone begging in front of the Kop; four minutes later, his misery was exacerbated.

"He's GOT to hit the target!" Yasin Ayari missed a golden chance to put Brighton ahead against Liverpool 🫣 https://t.co/Qz7G3sXCpP.

Liverpool’s lead was secured with an element of good fortune but, equally, the tenacity of Ronald Araújo and Wirtz was instrumental in pressing Brighton back to the point that they were panicking; Wirtz’s shot, deflected off Pascal Gross past Bart Verbruggen, compounded it all.

Recent findings suggest that “I think everyone in the stadium – and you as well – felt there was a missed opportunity for us,” groaned Fabian Hürzeler, the visitors’ head coach. “It’s not only after the goal or the goals they scored. Before they scored, we had two significant chances. I think it was just the difference that they scored and we didn’t score.”.

It would be wrong to say Wirtz was doing cartwheels – perhaps he knew immediately he would not get the goal – but it was an vital moment for him and you could feel the sense of goodwill towards him from team-mates and supporters alike.

Remarkably, this was the first time Liverpool had scored in the first half at Anfield in a Premier League fixture since May 9 and, with that momentum, it led to one of those periods when they started attacking in waves and carried the crowd with them.

What they needed was a second goal to arrive quite swiftly and that is what happened when Barcola won possession, scuttled forward and played a perfectly weighted bobbling ball into Isak’s path; the Swede did the rest, calmly finishing from eight yards.

In a recent development, everything with Isak feels to be going under the radar at the moment, but that is six goals in six Premier League appearances. He is starting to show the consistency and killer instinct that everyone felt he would. Iraola will be hoping it continues for the foreseeable future.

“The performance was really good,” said Isak, the quiet assassin. “We were really solid against a really good team. The first half is what we really want to be about. It was about intensity, winning balls and countering.”.

According to recent reports, brighton, as much as Hürzeler protested, could not properly recover, though this is no criticism. They remain committed to attack, they struck the frame of the goal when Ayari tried to punish an Alisson Becker mistake and the desire to keep pushing ensured Liverpool could never relax.

What Liverpool had going for them this time, however, was an intensity to preserve a clean sheet and nobody embodied the indefatigability more than Araújo, the Uruguay international whose loan from Barcelona is looking an increasingly shrewd piece of business.

Two moments stood out: one thunderous tackle on substitute Malick Yalcouyé in front of the Main Stand that had the locals roaring their approval, another in the first half when he was on the floor but still managed to head away to thwart Maxim De Cuyper.

They remember those moments as much as the stardust that Barcola and Isak provide. Put it all together and it might just be a launchpad for Iraola.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fondazione Milan will be the Match Charity Partner for AC Milan vs. Frosinone on Sunday, and Matteo Gabbia has spoken as part of the initiative.

According to recent reports, since 2003, the Foundation has used sport as a tool for change, reaching more than 200,000 young people through 288 projects in Italy and 25 other countries. More than €13m has been invested over the years on various projects to help those that are less fortunate.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Recent findings suggest that before kick-off on Sunday, the beneficiaries of the various schemes will take a photo with the starting lineup. They will also take part in pitch-side activities alongside Massimo Ambrosini, Daniele Massaro and Matteo Gabbia, who recently visited the Calcio Seduto project. Gabbia spoke at the event.

“It’s not easy to sum up in just a few minutes what Franco (Baresi) was like as a person and as a player. He was a key figure for the entire AC Milan club, for us kids who are trying to live up to him, and above all for all those people who always told me about his games.

“It’s always exciting for me to hear people talk about Franco and what he achieved with these colours, as a player and as a man.

Recent findings suggest that “I think Franco is a legend. Fondazione Milan embodies all the beauty and importance that Baresi had. I was moved when I met and got to know the kids from the sitting football team last week.

“I’m sure that if Franco had been there, he would have been proud of everything he organized and created for this foundation.”.

A post shared by Fondazione Milan (@fondazionemilan).

“I’m feeling better. It was a strange start to the season, and I was a bit disappointed personally. Hopefully, from the moment I return, it can be a positive season for me too.”.

The pregame will also honour the memory of Franco Baresi and his bond with Fondazione Milan. He was a dedicated supporter of its projects, including as a member of its Board of Directors. Club employees will take part in the tribute, along with his longtime teammate and friend Daniele Massaro.

At Sunday’s match, fans can continue to support the Foundation’s projects through donations and auctions of players’ shirts, helping create newly introduced opportunities for other young people.
